name: ANAD
full_title: Arabic Natural Audio Dataset
status_note: A recipe exists but is on hold. 768 near-identical clips (two groups of 386 and 382 that appear under different videos and labels) were excluded after listening, but every one of the remaining 566 also contains the same female voice ("ava smi...") with slightly different background sound; the cause is unknown. Labels are per video and their correspondence to chunks is unverified. Not used for training; to be re-checked if used for evaluation (maintainer's decision, 2026-10-23).
language_note: Arabic (phone-in callers on talk shows). Dialect not checked
license_note: Kaggle license field: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
labels_discrete_note: Labels are constant per video (call): V1, V3, V8 = happy; V2, V6 = surprised; V4, V5, V7 = angry. The release has 1,334 clips with both label and wav (the table has 1,383 rows): angry 723, happy 469, surprised 142. The 566 clips used by the recipe are angry 404, happy 154, surprise 8, almost all from two videos, V7 (angry 376) and V8 (happy 149).
label_basis_note: Eight live phone calls on Arabic talk shows. 18 listeners chose for each video whether they perceived happy, angry or surprised (the per-video label is copied to every 1-second chunk). Whether raters also watched the video is not stated ("listen to each video").
lexical_confound_note: Live talk-show calls, so what is said is not controlled. Labels are per video and copied to every 1-second chunk. Not measured (no transcripts).
annotations_other: Video (.avi), CSV of 950-dimensional acoustic features
notes: Samira Klaylat (Kaggle uploader) et al. Eight live calls from Arabic talk shows were downloaded, split at speaker turns, and 18 listeners chose among happy, angry and surprised. Silence, laughter and noise were removed and the rest automatically cut into 1-second units: 1,384 clips. A CSV of 950-dimensional acoustic features is included. Kaggle version v11 (2017-12-01). Paper: Klaylat, Osman, Hamandi, Zantout, Emotion recognition in Arabic speech, Analog Integrated Circuits and Signal Processing 96(2), 337-351 (2018) (bibliography checked via Crossref; full text not read). No speaker IDs. Two groups of 386 and 382 clips appear with near-identical sound under different videos and labels (the maintainer listened to 6 and confirmed). The recipe (egs3/anad/cls, on hold) uses the 566 clips without these 768; split train 396 / valid 56 / test 114 (after the length filter 349 / 33 / 114), max_epochs 273. No health check after the exclusion. Two short groups (0.29 s and 0.31 s) were not excluded.

name: Audio Speech Sentiment
status_note: Not usable. Labels are sentiment (positive / negative / neutral) and match the polarity of the meaning of the sentence read (all recordings of the same sentence have the same label). Unsuitable for learning paralinguistic information and unusable for categorical emotion classification; since the sentiment lives in the words, it is not useful for a speech sentiment task either. The 110 TEST clips have no labels.
language_note: English (from Whisper large-v3 language identification and the maintainer's listening; a light check only, no human-verified transcripts). Detection confidence is lowish, and the maintainer heard an Indian accent. The uploader does not state the language.
license_note: Kaggle license field: CC0. No source, author or recording information; the uploader's rights are unverified.
labels_discrete_note: negative 87, positive 82, neutral 81 (250 TRAIN clips). Polarity of the sentence meaning, not emotion.
label_basis_note: The Kaggle description says nothing about how the audio was recorded or labelled. Measured: all recordings of the same sentence carry the same polarity label (67 sentences, 145 clips), and labels match the polarity of the sentence content (review of 2026-10-22).
lexical_confound_note: Sentiment labels follow the polarity of the sentence; every repeated sentence has one label (Whisper transcripts). Excluded for this reason.
annotations_other: Sentiment labels, mel-spectrogram images
sheet_notes: The Kaggle uploader labels the dataset CC0, but no original source, collection procedure, speaker consent, publication, or evidence of the uploader's authority to license the audio was identified. Audio rights and provenance remain unverified.
notes: Speech sentiment data on Kaggle. 250 TRAIN clips (labels in `TRAIN.csv`), 110 TEST clips (no labels), 360 mel-spectrogram PNG images. wav 44.1 kHz stereo (240 PCM_16, 120 64-bit float), 1.698-3.944 s (TRAIN total 0.184 h). No duplicates. The following comes only from light checks (Whisper large-v3 transcripts, F0 distribution, the maintainer's listening), not human verification: English sentences (67 sentences used in 145 clips, every recording of a sentence has the same label); probably a single speaker (F0 5th-95th percentile 128-148 Hz). No information on speakers, gender, sentences, origin, authors or labelling procedure. Whether the voice was acted to match the sentence polarity was not checked.

name: BARI-EmoSpeech
full_title: BARI-EmoSpeech: A Dialect-Specific Speech Emotion Recognition Dataset for Barishal Bangla
status_note: Not used: no voice difference between emotions could be heard, and emotions appear to be separated by sentence content (maintainer's listening 2026-10-23, confirmed with 100 Whisper transcripts). Officially 5 speakers, but listening and a speaker model suggest one person. Both checks were provisional and of low reliability.
license_note: Mendeley Data license field: CC BY 4.0.
label_basis_note: The distributor says the utterances are spontaneous and were collected with culturally relevant prompts (e.g. festival memories for happiness). Labels come from dual annotation (Fleiss' kappa = 0.82). However, listening found no voice difference between emotions; emotions appear to be separated by sentence content (excluded in the review of 2026-10-23).
lexical_confound_note: Emotion-themed prompts produce emotion-matching content (e.g. sadness: 'the happy days are over'); no voice difference was heard. Excluded for this reason.
paralinguistic_signal_note: The maintainer listened on 2026-10-23 and could not hear a voice difference between emotions; all clips sounded like the same voice. Provisional, low reliability (a light listening). The dataset is not used.
notes: Mendeley Data hpfv67fgb8 version 1 (2025-10-10, Daffodil International University). Barishal-dialect Bengali, 5 emotions (Affection, Happiness, Jealousy, Normal, Sadness). The description promises 16 kHz WAV, a train/val split and a CSV (speaker, duration), but the release is 2,312 m4a files (AAC etc.) in emotion folders with no split and no CSV. "Five native Barishal speakers (aged 22-45, gender-balanced) collected samples" can mean they spoke or that they collected. On listening, all clips sound like the same (child-like) female voice, and a speaker model (ESPnet-SPK SKA-TDNN trained on VoxCeleb; EER 24% on the reference SUBESCO) puts 2,204 of 2,303 clips (96%) in one cluster. The 99 outliers (70 of them normal) were not listened to. No voice difference between emotions could be heard, and transcripts show the sentence content itself expresses the emotion (e.g. sadness: "the happy days are over"; affection: "don't look at your phone while eating"). Therefore not used. The speaker and content checks were provisional and of low reliability (2026-10-23). Whisper language ID also gives mostly bn (94% of the 682 clips with confidence >= 0.9).

name: BASER
full_title: Bangla Adolescent Speech Emotion Recognition
status_note: Implemented with 5 classes (angry / fear / happy / neutral / sad). Uses 692 clips after removing 58 duplicates of the same sound (confirmed by the maintainer's listening).
license_note: Kaggle license field: Apache 2.0 (checked by the maintainer on 2026-10-23). Includes minors aged 12-19 with no statement of consent; by the maintainer's decision this is not treated as a problem.
label_basis_note: Acted by non-professional actors aged 12-19. Labels are the emotions acted (file names). No listening check is described.
lexical_confound_note: The same 5 sentences in every emotion (Whisper sample of 2 of 10 speakers; sentence texts are not distributed).
notes: Md Jabed Hossain. 12 non-professional adolescent actors aged 12-19. The description does not list the emotions. Kaggle `jabedcse/baser-dataset` (version 1, 2023-12-16, author Md Jabed Hossain). Acted Bengali speech. The description says 12 non-professional actors aged 12-19 (6 male, 6 female), but the release has 10 speakers (5 female: CHAITY, IRA, MAHI, TABASSUM, Tahsin; 5 male: HASAN, MIFTA, MAHMUD, RIAD, JUHAYER); the reason is unknown (as of 2026-10-23). Each speaker: 5 sentences x 5 emotions (angry, fear, happy, neutral, sad) x 3 takes = 75 clips; 750 in total (150 per emotion), 48 kHz mono 16-bit, 1.714-5.013 s, 0.6059 h. No sentence texts (transcripts). The Kaggle page cites no paper. 58 of the 750 clips duplicate the same sound (speaker RIAD has byte-identical takes in all 25 groups (50 redundant), plus 7 clips in 6 other groups, plus 1 clip with a different byte stream but the same waveform); confirmed by the maintainer's listening. The recipe keeps the lowest take of each group and uses 692 clips.

name: BERSt
full_title: B(asic) E(motion) R(andom phrase) S(hou)t(s)
status_note: Implemented with 7 classes (angry / disgust / fear / happy / neutral / sad / surprise). Uses 4,460 clips after removing 63: byte-identical duplicates, groups with conflicting metadata, and clips containing several takes (maintainer's decision, 2026-10-23).
language_note: English (regional accents from the UK, Canada, US and Australia, and non-native speakers of French, Russian, Hindi, etc.)
license_note: Hugging Face card: CC BY 4.0.
label_basis_note: 98 professional actors performed phrases at three levels: speaking, raising the voice and shouting. Labels are the emotions given to the actors; the card states they were not validated through perception.
lexical_confound_note: Parallel nonsense phrases, so the script carries no emotion. But some clips start with the spoken emotion name (3 of 86 long clips; short clips not checked), which leaks the label in words.
notes: Rosie Lab (Simon Fraser University). Computer Speech & Language 2025 (arXiv 2505.00059). 98 professional actors recorded at home on smartphones, 19 phone positions, three vocal intensity levels (speak, raise voice, shout), 13 nonsense phrases covering all phonemes. Release quality issues (2026-10-23): (1) 31 groups, 82 clips of byte-identical audio (24 groups: the same sound in different recordings of the same speaker, emotion and phrase; 2 groups: different chunks of the same recording; 5 groups: carry metadata of different speakers, emotions or phrases, one of them spanning valid and test). (2) Some clips still contain all three vocal levels (A, B, C) in one file (the phrase repeated three times; the recordist apparently recorded the three levels together and forgot to cut them). (3) Some start with the spoken emotion name ("Anger."). (2) and (3) were found from Whisper transcripts of the 86 clips longer than 6 s; the ~4,437 clips of 6 s or less were not checked. Trimming individual clips would make them usable, but by the maintainer's decision the problems are only documented in the readme. The recipe uses 4,460 clips after removing the 63 duplicates, conflicting and multi-take clips. 3,704 clips at 48 kHz and 819 at 44.1 kHz, mono 16-bit, 1.028-22.528 s, 3.7248 h in total. Official split (train 78, valid 10, test 10 speakers; no speaker overlap).

name: CASIA
status_note: [WARNING] The recipe's data source (a Hugging Face mirror) is an unofficial redistribution of a corpus licensed for a fee and should not be used. The distributor ChineseLDC (CLDC-SPC-2005-010) licenses it for a fee (archived page of 2020-05-01: from CNY 5,000 domestic non-commercial to CNY 105,000 foreign commercial). The widely used 1,200-clip version (EmoBox etc.) is a re-upload by an individual to Baidu AI Studio on 2023-04-16, and the Hugging Face mirror was confirmed to hold the same files (size and modification time match for 20 files). No source allows free redistribution. Tao et al. 2008, which SER papers cite for it, describes a single-speaker speech-synthesis corpus and does not mention emotion. No paper by the creators was found. The recipe is kept with a warning by the maintainer's decision (2026-10-23). Details: reports/2026-10-23_casia_db_update.md.
license_note: Paid license from ChineseLDC (page archived 2020-05-01: domestic research CNY 5,000, domestic commercial 15,000, foreign research 35,000, foreign commercial 105,000). Terms as of 2024 unverified (the site could not be reached). None of the sources read allows free redistribution. The license field of the original AI Studio upload of the 1,200-clip version says 其他 (other); the LICENSE file of the Hugging Face mirror is 0 bytes.
labels_discrete_note: The 2010 edition (9,600 sentences) states only the number, 六种情绪 (six emotions), without listing them. The 2005 annotation guide has 5 emotions (高兴, 悲哀, 生气, 惊吓, 中性), which does not match six. The 1,200-clip version has 6 emotions (angry, fear, happy, neutral, sad, surprise), consistent between the file names and the AI Studio description.
label_basis_note: Speakers (2 male, 2 female) read identical sentences and emotion-revealing sentences in each emotion (ChineseLDC 2005 annotation guide). Labels are the target emotion read. No listening check is described. The same holds for the 1,200-clip version used by the recipe.
lexical_confound_note: Whole corpus: 40% (2005 guide) or 25% (2010 page) of sentences reveal the emotion by meaning. The recipe's 1,200-clip version holds sentence numbers 201-250; 201-205 are the same sentence in every emotion (Whisper), the rest unverified.
annotations_other: speaker metadata
sheet_notes: Acted Mandarin emotional speech from four professional speakers. Access is paid/restricted; the 1,200-utterance subset is the configuration used by the EmoBox benchmark.
notes: "CASIA汉语情感语料库" (CASIA Chinese emotional speech corpus) of the Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences (ChineseLDC CLDC-SPC-2005-010, developed 2005, added to ChineseLDC 2008-06-11, updated 2010-10-09). Acted speech: 4 professional speakers (2 male, 2 female) read identical sentences and sentences whose meaning reveals the emotion, with emotion; 16 kHz, 16-bit PCM. The size differs by edition (2005 catalogue: 6 emotions, 12,000 sentences / annotation guide: 5 emotions, 10,000 sentences; resource page updated 2010: 6 emotions, 9,600 sentences). The full corpus includes .tag files with syllable boundaries and F0. No paper by the creators was found. Tao, Liu, Zhang, Jia, "Design of Speech Corpus for Mandarin Text to Speech" (Blizzard Challenge 2008), cited by SER papers, describes a single-female-speaker 5,000-sentence speech-synthesis corpus and does not mention emotion (full text read). The 1,200-clip version used by EmoBox and others (4 speakers x 6 emotions x sentence numbers 201-250) was re-uploaded on 2023-04-16 to Baidu AI Studio (dataset 209512) by an individual (display name 千鹤) who is not the creator. The recipe's Hugging Face mirror (Bill13579/casia-mirror, created 2025-06-29, LICENSE 0 bytes) holds the same files: size and modification time match the 20 files shown on AI Studio (not checked by hash). No statement allowing free redistribution was found. Full investigation: reports/2026-10-23_casia_db_update.md.

name: C-BESD
full_title: Children-Bilingual Emotion Speech Dataset
status_note: Implemented with 6 classes (angry / disgust / fear / happy / neutral / sad), Telugu and English. Uses 4,164 of the 4,204 released clips; 40 are removed: 10 misplaced copies, 1 " - Copy", 2 with the same sound under different labels, and 27 second-or-later copies of the same sound under the same label (the last 27 by the maintainer's decision, 2026-10-23).
license_note: Kaggle license field: CC BY-SA 4.0 (checked by the maintainer on 2026-10-23; the DB maintainer also checked via the API). The description says nothing about consent for recording children; by the maintainer's decision the license is the basis.
label_basis_note: Children aged 6-12 read simple sentences in each emotion (recorded with SurveyLex). Labels are the emotion recorded (folder and file names). No listening check is described.
lexical_confound_note: Children read emotion-matching sentences (English sample of 90 clips by Whisper); the Telugu half was not checked. A model may learn the words.
notes: Kaggle `pranuthi19/bilingual-emotion-speech-datasetbesd` (version 1, 2024-02-07, author pranuthi_19). 70 children aged 6-12 (35 boys, 35 girls; 10 per age), native Telugu speakers learning English as a second language, recorded with SurveyLex. Telugu and English, 6 emotions, 5 utterances per emotion. File names `child number.language+gender_age_emotion_utterance number` (stated in the description). The description gives both 4,320 and 4,200 utterances; 4,320 is an arithmetic slip, since its own formula (35 x 2 x 5 x 6 x 2) gives 4,200. It also says 30 utterances per child, while the formula implies 60. The release has 4,204 wav files, 48 kHz stereo 16-bit, 3.0321 h in total (the description says about 2.5 h). The same child number appears only in some emotion folders, so recordings cannot be grouped by child. 36 groups (75 files) are byte-identical: 10 groups cross emotion folders (9 are misplaced folder copies, 1 is the same sound under neutral and sad) and 1 is " - Copy". The remaining 25 groups (52 files) share a label; 23 carry different child numbers, 5 of them different ages (e.g. neutral utterances 1-5 exist both for child 50, age 8, and child 70, age 7). Which is correct cannot be told from the release (2026-10-23). The recipe uses 4,164 clips after removing the 13 misplaced, " - Copy" and cross-label files and the 27 second-or-later copies within same-label groups.

status_note: Implemented with 7 classes. Uses all 4,160 clips (the 15 train clips over 30 s are dropped by remove_long_short). The repository's NOTICE says it incorporates ESD (research use only), but no overlap with ESD's audio or sentences was found, so that condition is not applied and the data is treated as Apache-2.0 (open) per the card (maintainer's decision, 2026-10-23).
language_note: Mandarin Chinese. Speakers are native Mandarin speakers
license_note: The card and LICENSE say Apache-2.0. The repository's NOTICE (pinned commit 19498e62...) says it incorporates Emotional-Speech-Data (ESD, MIT) that "can only be used for research purpose", but does not say which clips, and the card does not mention ESD. No clip overlaps in sound with any of ESD's 35,000 clips (re-checked by the DB maintainer, 2026-10-23), and no sentence is close to ESD's 350 Mandarin sentences (at most 19% character-bigram overlap). The Marco-Voice report describes CSEMOTIONS as new recordings and lists ESD as separate training data. The NOTICE may stem from the whole project, but the authors do not explain it. Treated as open by the maintainer's decision. Details: reports/2026-10-23_csemotions_db_update.md.
label_basis_note: 10 professional voice actors performed 7 emotions in a studio. Labels are the emotions performed (emotion column). Neither the card nor the paper describes checking labels by listening (the paper's listening tests evaluate synthesised speech).
lexical_confound_note: Each script sentence occurs under one emotion only, so the text alone determines the label. The voice also differs by emotion (maintainer's listening).
paralinguistic_signal_note: The maintainer listened to 4 clips per emotion (different speakers) on 2026-10-23 and found paralinguistic information clearly present. Not a measurement.
notes: Alibaba AIDC-AI (named ATH-MaaS on Hugging Face). Released with the Marco-Voice technical report (arXiv 2508.02038). Studio recordings of 10 professional voice actors (5 male, 5 female), 7 emotions (neutral, happy, angry, sad, surprise, playfulness, fearful), 4,160 clips, 10.1978 h (measured), 1.752-34.212 s, 48 kHz mono 16-bit (the card says 24-bit; measured 16-bit). The `text` column holds the script sentence; 1,293 of 1,296 sentences are read by several speakers. Every sentence occurs under one emotion only, so the emotion can be read from the meaning (the maintainer listened to 4 clips per emotion and judged that the voice also differs by emotion, but a model may still use the meaning). No duplicates. The card's column names (transcript / speaker_id / gender / prompt_id) differ from the actual columns (audio / text / emotion / speaker). The paper says each speaker read 100 Chinese and English prompts, but the data has 1,296 distinct Chinese sentences. The paper's evaluation prompts are 100 per emotion (English and Chinese). For the NOTICE that mentions ESD, see license_note and reports/2026-10-23_csemotions_db_update.md.

status_note: [VALUABLE AS CONVERSATIONAL SPEECH] Keeps 2,541 two-person dialogues intact, with utterance order, topic, dialogue act and transcript (21.7 h). The current recipe does utterance-level SER without the dialogue structure, but the data may be needed for future dialogue research (dialogue-level emotion recognition, context-aware SER, conversational speech) (maintainer's assessment, 2026-10-24). Labels are DailyDialog's annotations of the text, which the voice actors followed; they were not assigned by listening to the audio. The recipe uses 23,772 utterances, leaving out the valid-side copy of one shared recording.
language_note: English. Two actors fluent in English who had lived in the US for at least 3 years
license_note: The README says data and code are freely available for academic use under CC-BY-SA 4.0 (the repository license field says MIT).
release_version: GitHub release (link in the README, downloaded 2026-10-20)
labels_discrete_note: Inherits DailyDialog's labels (no emotion, anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise). Values per the DailyDialog paper
label_basis_note: Two voice actors fluent in English recorded DailyDialog dialogues as conversations in a studio and were directed to follow each utterance's emotion label. Those labels are DailyDialog's annotations of the text (from context and meaning), which DailyTalk inherits. No listening check is described.
lexical_confound_note: Labels were assigned from the written dialogue, so the words carry the label by construction (about 80% of utterances are 'no emotion'). Not measured; transcripts are in metadata.json.
annotations_other: DailyDialog dialogue acts and topics; whether fillers (uh, um) were added
notes: Lee, Park, Kim (KAIST, arXiv 2207.01063, ICASSP 2023). Conversational (dialogue-structured) speech data. 2,541 dialogues selected from DailyDialog were recorded in a studio by two voice actors fluent in English, as real conversations (not read verbatim from the script; they were directed to follow each utterance's emotion label). The release has 23,773 wav files (44.1 kHz, 16-bit; 23,720 mono, 53 stereo) and metadata.json, 21.6740 h in total. 7 labels (no emotion 18,966, happiness 3,856, surprise 407, sadness 301, anger 159, disgust 66, fear 18). metadata.json gives dialogue number, turn order, topic (1-10), dialogue act (inform 10,611, question 7,050, directive 3,741, commissive 2,371), transcript and speaker (0 / 1). The paper counts dialogues with added fillers (uh, um) as 962 for speaker 0 and 689 for speaker 1 (the release does not mark which). The paper says dialogues with more than 5 turns were selected, but the shortest dialogue in the data has 5 utterances. One utterance uses the same recording in two dialogues (d1121-u009 and d1253-u009, byte-identical), and 4 pairs of dialogues have identical text (177 and 532, 288 and 1698, 507 and 1383, 1069 and 2047; recorded separately).

name: EESC
full_title: Estonian Emotional Speech Corpus
status_note: Implemented with 4 classes (angry / happy / neutral / sad); uses all 1,164 clips. Labels are what listeners perceived, not the speaker's intent: the reader was given no emotion and the passages' content was meant to evoke it. The words may have driven both the reader and the listeners; the authors' content-influence flag is not in the release (2026-10-24).
license_note: figshare: CC BY 4.0. META-SHARE (doi:10.15155/EKI.000A) says Licence CC-BY (no version) and Availability: Available - Restricted Use.
label_basis_note: At least 30 Estonians over 30 who had lived in Estonia heard each sentence in isolation, without the text, and chose sadness, anger, joy or neutral; a sentence counts as identified when more than 50% chose the same (908 of 1,234). The listeners understood the words. Per-sentence identification rates are on the corpus site, not in the figshare release. How the release labels the 326 sentences without a majority is not described.
lexical_confound_note: The passages were chosen because readers saw the emotion in the text, and the listeners understood the words. The authors' 14 text-only reading tests (10+ readers each, no audio) agree with the listeners for 515 of the 908 identified sentences (57%; paper Table 2). The release (figshare) does not carry this content-influence flag, so the two groups cannot be separated in the recipe.
annotations_other: perception rate
sheet_notes: Read emotional speech from one female speaker. The corpus includes perceived-emotion and valence judgments; an explicit reusable license was not confirmed.
notes: Altrov & Pajupuu (ES3 workshop at LREC 2012, pp. 50-53), Institute of the Estonian Language (Eesti Keele Instituut); Estonian name Eesti emotsionaalse kõne korpus (EEKK). One female reader, chosen for articulation, a pleasant voice and empathy, read 130 journalistic passages without being told an emotion; the passages had been chosen because readers agreed they carried joy, anger or sadness. The passages were cut into sentences, and each sentence's label was set by a listening test (see label_basis_note). The paper also describes a text-only reading test that flags whether content may have influenced identification; the corpus site (peeter.eki.ee:5000, unreachable on 2026-10-24) shows that flag and per-sentence rates, the figshare release does not. Release: 1,164 wav (44.1 kHz mono 16-bit, 1.0850 h, 0.445-14.011 s) with TextGrids (tiers phoneme, word, sentence, emotion; 469 also have pos). Labels in the release: neutral 338, anger 306, joy 271, sadness 249, which do not match the paper's identified counts (joy 232, anger 277, sadness 191, neutral 208; 326 unidentified). 1,083 distinct sentence texts: 80 occur more than once (161 clips) and 27 of those carry different labels (e.g. 'Nii enda kui ka teiste puhul.' as neutral and anger). No byte-identical files.

name: EMIS
full_title: Emotionally Incongruent Synthetic Speech Dataset
status_note: Synthetic speech from three zero-shot TTS systems (F5-TTS, CosyVoice2, StyleTTS2) imitating ESD English speakers; sentences are built so the emotion in the words usually differs from the emotion in the voice. The label is the voice emotion requested of the TTS, not a perceived emotion (a 40-listener check on a subset found 39.4-62.0% identification). Materials carry research-only and non-commercial conditions (see license_note). Whether to use synthetic data in experiments is not decided here (2026-10-24).
license_note: Zenodo record license: GPL-3.0-or-later (checked by the maintainer, 2026-10-24). The audio was synthesised from ESD reference voices by three TTS systems; the record and the paper do not discuss their terms. Read on 2026-10-24: ESD has an MIT LICENSE file, but its README asks users to sign a license form and says the database can only be used for research purpose. The F5-TTS code is MIT while its pre-trained models are CC-BY-NC (trained on Emilia, CC BY-NC-4.0 with YODAS part CC BY 4.0, access requires accepting conditions). CosyVoice2 code and model are Apache-2.0 on the model card, but its paper says the training data came from internal tools and does not name the sources. StyleTTS2 code is MIT; its README asks users of the pre-trained models to tell listeners that speech is synthesised unless the voice owner permitted it. Which checkpoints EMIS used, and how model terms reach generated audio, is not stated. Whether GPL-3.0-or-later overrides these conditions is not stated either.
label_basis_note: Label = the voice emotion requested of the TTS system, taken from the emotion of the ESD reference audio (the third field from the end of the file name). Not perceived: the release has no per-clip listener data. The paper's 40-listener check covers a balanced subset only (identification of the reference emotion 39.4-62.0% for the three TTS systems, 70.8% for ground-truth samples; arXiv v2, ICASSP version not seen).
lexical_confound_note: Every sentence is synthesised in all four voice emotions by all three TTS systems, so the words carry no information about the label. The text emotion (explicit, implicit or neutral) is in the file name and agrees with the label in only 312 of 1,248 files (25%).
notes: Corrêa, Lima, Moreno, Ueda, Costa (UNICAMP). Paper: arXiv 2510.25054 (Zenodo links the ICASSP 2026 DOI 10.1109/ICASSP55912.2026.11462441, whose text was not seen). Synthetic speech. 104 emotion-rich sentences written by GPT-4.5 (the Zenodo record says ChatGPT-4.5): per emotion (angry, happy, sad) explicit and implicit sentences, plus neutral sentences; each was synthesised in four voice emotions (angry, happy, neutral, sad) by F5-TTS, CosyVoice2 and StyleTTS2 (named in the paper; file names say F5TTS, COSY, STYLE). Reference audio: for each generation one of the 10 ESD English speakers (0011-0020) was drawn at random and their 7 longest utterances concatenated (about 30 s). 1,248 files (416 per TTS), 24 kHz mono, 1.2629 h, 1.824-8.107 s; F5TTS files are PCM_16 and the others float. 936 files have a voice emotion different from the text emotion and 312 are congruent. 26 sentence groups (number at the start of the file name): groups 01-13 hold six emotional sentences and one neutral sentence, groups 14-26 one neutral sentence each. No byte-identical files. text_samples_EMIS.csv in the record lists the sentences. The 'ground-truth' samples of the paper's listening check are not described. EMIS derives its reference voices from ESD (no relation row: the vocabulary has no derived_from type).

name: EmoGator
full_title: EmoGator: A New Open Source Vocal Burst Dataset
status_note: Implemented with 30 classes (vocal bursts); uses all 32,130 clips including 20 byte-identical pairs. Labels are the category the speaker meant to express; no listener rated them. Quality control was done by one person (the paper's author), who judged from a North American English perspective.
license_note: GitHub license field: Apache-2.0.
label_basis_note: Label = the category of the prompt the contributor was answering (the speaker's intent). No listener ratings exist. Quality control by one person (the paper's author): silent or noise-only submissions and readings of category names were handled, problematic samples re-recorded, and contributors who did not convey distinct emotions left out (how many is not stated).
lexical_confound_note: Non-speech vocal bursts. Whisper transcripts of 600 random clips (20 per category) are mostly interjections (Ah, Aww, Hmm, Ugh); no clip contains a category name and 3 contain two or more ordinary words (e.g. 'You're weird.'). Not a full-corpus check; no person verified the transcripts.
notes: Fred W. Buhl (University of Florida, arXiv 2301.00508). Unpaid volunteers and Mechanical Turk workers recorded each of 30 categories 3 times (90 per person) after reading prompts that describe a situation for the category (a modified and expanded version of the prompts of the Hume-VB study; listed in the paper's online supplement, which was not read), on a website using their own devices. Files are mp3 (the paper says 44.1 or 48 kHz; measured 48 kHz mono 30,334, 48 kHz stereo 1,706, 44.1 kHz mono 90), 0.420-2.040 s, 16.7667 h measured (the paper says 16.9654 h, possibly a different way of measuring mp3 length). File names are <six-digit contributor ID>-<category 01-30>-<take 1-3>. 357 contributors with 90 files each; 1,071 files per category. 20 byte-identical pairs (same contributor and category, different takes). All participants gave informed consent and the procedure was approved by the University of Florida IRB (paper). The author warns of a bias toward North American English speakers' expressions. Contributor sex, age, language and origin are not in the release. Efforts were made to avoid one person contributing twice, without a guarantee. The paper suggests the data could be used to measure how often listeners identify the intended category.

status_note: The audio is synthetic (GPT-4 OmniAudio, 11 voices, 4 languages). The 12,600 Bench items were rated by 2-4 of 6 psychology experts; about 4.7k were unanimous (abstract). EmoNet-Voice Big is synthetic speech for pre-training (the abstract says 5,000 hours; the per-language sum in Table 2 is 4,752 hours; Table 1 says >1M items and >4,500 hours). EmoNet-Voice Bench is an evaluation set of 12,600 items (36.26 hours) chosen from Big; 6 experts (psychology bachelor or higher) gave 33,605 ratings (2-4 per item). The abstract's 4.7k is the unanimous part. Inter-rater Cronbach's alpha is 0.14. It includes, through synthesis, emotions that are hard to collect from people, such as pain and shame. Distributed through the paper's Hugging Face collection laion/emonet: emonet-voice-bench (12,600 items, CC-BY-4.0) and emonet-voice-foundation under the anonymous account t1a5anu-anon. The foundation card points to laion/laions_got_talent_enhanced_flash_annotations_and_long_captions as the main data. The paper says it is released as a research artefact for academic use.

name: EmoSpeech (keyword)
status_note: Implemented with 4 classes (angry / calm / fear / happy); uses 6,530 of the 7,735 clips. The 1,116 `background` clips are left out: they hold only environmental sound, no speech (the maintainer listened, 2026-10-24), although they carry emotion tags. The one clip with emotion None and 88 duplicates are also left out. Keywords are not spread evenly over emotions (see lexical_confound_note).
language_note: Keywords (help, bacho, stop, ...). Language not stated
license_note: Kaggle license field: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The bundled License.txt is Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 International, and the paper says the data is released for non-commercial purposes (checked by the maintainer, 2026-10-24).
label_basis_note: Label = the emotion displayed to the speaker (calm, happy, angry, fearful). Reviewers matched each recording against reference samples (paper Section 4.4); no ratings are distributed. The `background` class carries the same emotion tags although it holds no speech.
lexical_confound_note: All keywords occur under every emotion (parallel), but not evenly: the help-type words (bacho, help) are mostly fearful (47% and 42%), stop/go/yes/no are 18-26% angry or fearful, and `unknown` is 88% calm. Cramer's V between keyword and emotion is 0.30 (file-name counts, 2026-10-25). The words therefore carry some information about the label.
notes: Indian EmoSpeech Command Dataset (Banga, Upadhyay, Agarwal, Sharma, Mukherjee, arXiv 1910.13801, 2019). Kaggle ujjwal9/emospeech (free account). 3-second commands recorded on phones in real surroundings (house, metro, roads, railway, near a lake, ...), each with a keyword, an emotion and an environment sound. Keyword classes: help, bachao (spelled bacho in the files), stop, go, yes, no, `unknown` (any other word) and `background` (sound whose source is not human vocal chords, e.g. birds or road noise; paper Section 5). Emotions: calm, happy, angry, fearful, and a tag None. Environment tag in the file name: safe, scream, glass break, gunshots (the README does not list scream). Collection: Android app, then a game-like web app; 250 speakers (paper); privacy-policy consent. Quality control: samples whose word reviewers cannot tell are rejected, each sample is checked by two people, and emotion is matched against reference samples (Section 4.4). Release: 7,735 wav (16 kHz mono 16-bit, 1.963-3.755 s, 6.5486 h), README.md, License.txt; names are keyword-environment-emotion-timestamp-hash.wav; 89 groups of byte-identical files (179 files, 90 redundant). `background` has 1,116 clips (calm 880, None 163, fearful 53, happy 19, angry 1); `None` has 164 clips, 163 of them background. The hash field has 103 values and does not match the paper's 250 speakers. Language is not stated (English and Hindi words).

name: EmoTale
full_title: EmoTale: An Enacted Speech-emotion Dataset in Danish
status_note: Implemented with 5 classes (angry / boredom / happy / neutral / sad); uses all 800 clips. No license text: the datasheet says copyright, no license, and asks to cite the paper, which is treated as the terms of use (maintainer's decision, 2026-10-26; asking the authors is optional). The recipe trains on the enacted emotion; the three annotators' perceived labels exist in annotations.csv and are not used.
license_note: The repository (snehadas/EmoTale, commit 41e7d00f) has no LICENSE file and GitHub shows no license. The datasheet answers 'Will the dataset be distributed under a copyright or other IP license?' with: 'The data will be distributed under a copyright. There is no license, but there is a request to cite the corresponding paper if the dataset is used.' The project treats the request to cite the paper as the terms of use (the maintainer's decision, 2026-10-26), as for IESC, so the class is open. The authors have not been asked; confirming with them is optional.
label_basis_note: Main label = the emotion the participant was asked to enact (file name; equals gt_emotion in annotations.csv for all 800). In addition, three annotators (the first, second and last authors of the paper) independently gave each utterance a categorical emotion and arousal, valence and dominance on a 1-5 scale in 0.5 steps; these are in annotations.csv and agree with the enacted emotion in 639, 706 and 507 of 800 cases. Cohen's kappa against the enacted emotion is 0.75 and 0.85 for annotators 1 and 2 (paper Table II). All three agree in 465 clips, at least two in 749 (113 of them differ from the enacted emotion), and none agree in 51.
lexical_confound_note: Five emotionally neutral sentences (translated from Emo-DB), each enacted in every emotion by every participant, so the words carry no label information.
annotations_other: Emotion categories and arousal, valence, dominance (1-5 in steps of 0.5) by 2 annotators
notes: Hjuler, Skat-Rørdam, Clemmensen, Das (DTU, ASRU 2025, arXiv 2508.14548; collected as part of a master's thesis). Enacted speech in Danish and English. Participants with acting experience were recruited (age at least 7, Danish speakers); recorded in quiet rooms with wireless Rode microphones at 48 kHz (stereo 16-bit wav in the release). 18 participants (12 female, 6 male, 9-39 years, mean 22.8; 3 are children aged 9-12) enacted 5 emotionally neutral sentences (translated from Emo-DB) in 5 emotions (anger, happiness, sadness, boredom, neutral), self-inducing the emotion by recalling a situation; only the last take was kept. 800 clips (450 Danish, 350 English), 160 per emotion, 1.070-7.443 s, 0.6170 h. File names: language_speaker_emotion_sentence (e.g. DK_004_A_5.wav). Written consent under GDPR, IRB approval (documents in the repository). The label is the enacted emotion; annotations.csv additionally holds three annotators' perceived categories and arousal-valence-dominance ratings (the annotators are three authors of the paper). The README says two annotators; the paper reports agreement between annotators 1 and 2 and the file holds three. The datasheet warns that the dataset is small and not suited for tasks needing large-scale training or natural emotional speech. The recipe does not use the perceived labels.

status_note: Implemented with 5 classes (neutral / angry / happy / sad / fear). Labels are the listeners' final labels (`best_emo`). Uses 953 clips.

They match the target emotion given to the speakers (file names) for 885 of 953 clips; 68 differ (fear -> angry 14, sad 6, neutral 4, happy 2; happy -> fear 9, neutral 9, sad 5, angry 2; etc.). Labels used: neutral 277, angry 182, sad 175, happy 160, fear 159.

The number of raters and how ratings were combined are not described in detail in the release. The recipe uses the final evaluation label (*_best_emo), not the target emotion.

annotations_other: Listener evaluations (emotion, strength, confidence), final labels, articulatory data
notes: EMA (electromagnetic articulography) corpus of USC SAIL. The Zenodo description gives the DOI of a 2005 paper and 4 emotions, 680 utterances, 10 sentences for women and 14 for the man, but the zip holds 5 emotions, 956 wav files (3 of them dummies), 8 sentences + 2 passages, which does not match. 3 speakers (jn, jr = female, kf = male). The zip's README says the speaker IDs (F1, F2, M1) are the same as in USC-EMO-MRI (possibly the same people; which corresponds to which is not documented; recorded here because relations has no suitable type; the maintainer judged it fine to include both in a multi-corpus set, 2026-10-22). wav are 22.05 kHz mono 16-bit (not the 16 kHz the README says); the 953 used clips are 1.359-63.0 s, 1.63 h in total. All 953 have listener evaluations (11, 13 or 15 ratings per utterance: per-listener emotion, strength and confidence, vote totals, final label). name: EmoVoice-DB
status_note: All audio is synthesised with OpenAI's GPT-4o-audio (texts and emotion descriptions with GPT-4o). The training data of that model is not public, and OpenAI's service terms may reach its output, so use needs to be considered in addition to the fact that the speech is synthetic (maintainer, 2026-10-24). Whether to use it is not decided here. Implemented with 7 classes; uses the 22,100 clips named in the official lists, not the 2,823 extra wav files.
license_note: Hugging Face card: MIT (checked by the maintainer, 2026-10-24). All audio is synthesised with OpenAI's GPT-4o-audio. The GPT-4o System Card (arXiv 2410.21276) says the pre-training data are selected public data (mainly industry-standard machine-learning datasets and web crawls) and proprietary data from partnerships, with multimodal data including images, audio and video; it names no datasets or sources, so the rights to the voices it learned from are unknown. The OpenAI Services Agreement (version effective 2026-01-01; read on 2026-10-25) says that between customer and OpenAI the customer owns all Output (4.1), and that the customer may not use Output to develop AI models that compete with OpenAI products and services except for permitted exceptions (3.3(e)): models mainly for categorising or classifying data (such as embeddings or classifiers) that are not distributed or made commercially available to third parties, and fine-tuning offered by OpenAI. Which terms applied to the API use when EmoVoice-DB was made (early 2025), and whether training a speech emotion recognizer counts under these terms, is not stated in any source read. The card and the paper do not mention OpenAI's terms. The GitHub README of the EmoVoice model (as recorded earlier) says the model weights are CC-BY-NC because of the Emilia training data; that is separate from the data license.
label_basis_note: Label = the coarse emotion category paired with the fine-grained description used as the instruction to GPT-4o-audio. Not perceived by any listener; the card describes no emotion check (only WER filtering).
lexical_confound_note: Each text was generated together with its emotion description, and the lists show almost no sentence under two emotions (14 of 21,952 distinct texts). The words therefore tend to reveal the label; synthetic voices add a second, unknown route.
annotations_other: Fine-grained natural-language emotion descriptions (generated by GPT-4o)
notes: Yang et al. (EmoVoice, arXiv 2504.12867, ACM MM 2025). English synthetic emotional speech; every clip generated by GPT-4o-audio. Steps (card and paper): (1) GPT-4o writes pairs of text (novel excerpts, dialogue, observations) and emotion description; (2) GPT-4o-audio is prompted with text and description (e.g. 'Repeat this sentence with the emotion of <description>: <text>') in one of 5 voices (ash, ballad, coral, sage, verse); (3) samples with high WER are removed; (4) GPT-4o rephrases each description twice, giving three descriptions per sample in train. 7 emotions: angry, happy, sad, surprised, disgusted, fearful, neutral. The official lists hold 22,100 clips (40.44 h; train 21,050, val 350, test 700; the train list has 63,150 rows because of the rephrasings); valid and test have equal counts per class. Archives: 24,923 wav (24 kHz mono 16-bit, 45.78 h, 1.05-59.6 s) in seven per-emotion zips, 2,823 of them in no list (5.34 h, all five voices; the reason is not stated). The five voices are synthetic timbres, not people. The Hugging Face repository also holds laions_got_latent.jsonl (203 MB), which the GitHub README of the model links to LAION's Got Talent; the recipe does not download it and no LAION file is among the wav. The card's text example for test.jsonl includes a neutral prompt speech file. Labels are the requested emotion, not perceived.

name: eNTERFACE
status_note: A recipe exists in egs3 (recipes.csv)
annotations_other: audiovisual recordings; nothing else shipped — demographics (81% male, 14 nationalities) only reported in the paper
sheet_notes: Each emotion category is performed using a different emotion-specific script, creating a deterministic correspondence between lexical content and emotion labels. Models trained on this corpus may therefore exploit linguistic cues rather than learn paralinguistic expression, so eNTERFACE should not be used as training data for paralinguistic learning. If included, it should be reserved for evaluation or robustness testing, with this lexical confound explicitly acknowledged because it may also inflate evaluation performance.
notes: The spreadsheet's 1,166 utterances cannot be traced to a source (the release has 1,293; the 42 complete subjects have 1,260). The release has no accompanying information, only AVI files and Thumbs.db. Labels and speakers are taken from directory names (the file names contain errors). The recipe drops subject 6 (an unsegmented session of one file per emotion, 56-107 s each) and uses the other 43 subjects, 1,287 of the 1,293 files; subject 23 lacks 3 recordings and its other 27 are used (recipe change of 2026-10-26). Scripts differ per emotion, so the emotion can be told from the words alone.

name: E-SERAVD
status_note: Implemented with the 6 classes of version 1.2. Uses 2,976 clips after removing 12 near-duplicate pairs (24 clips, the same sound under different labels).
license_note: The Kaggle page says CC BY 4.0. However, the material is dialogue audio from Indonesian films, and it is unlikely that the film rights holders allow free use (maintainer's judgement, 2026-10-22). The author's license field is trusted and the class stays `open`, but the doubt is recorded.
release_version: Three Kaggle releases (versions 1, 1.1, 1.2). Version 1.2 (6 emotions) is used
labels_discrete_note: Labels come from ratings by 3 people; the emotion whose mean probability is highest and at least 0.67 is the main emotion (README of version 1.2). The 3,000 clips are 500 per emotion. The README's vote counts (disgust 42 votes, fear 908 votes) cannot account for the final 500 disgust and 500 fear clips, and the README does not describe how these emotions were rated (an arithmetic reading, not confirmed with the authors). The recipe uses 2,976 clips after removing 24 near-duplicates.
label_basis_note: Dialogue from 11 Indonesian films (performed by actors). Each clip was rated by 3 raters over 6 emotions, and the emotion with mean probability >= 0.67 (at least 2 of 3) became the final label. Fleiss' kappa = 0.6713. The README only says "each audio and video clip was evaluated"; whether raters heard the audio only or also watched the video cannot be told.
lexical_confound_note: Film lines follow the scene, and raters may have used the words. Not measured (no transcripts).
annotations_other: Film abbreviation, 7 acoustic features (automatic)
notes: EEPIS (Electronic Engineering Polytechnic Institute of Surabaya). Version 1.2 (3,000 clips, 6 emotions) cut from dialogue in 11 Indonesian films. The files are 44.1 kHz stereo 32-bit float (the Kaggle page's "16 kHz" is wrong; the bundled specification sheet also says 44.1 kHz). 0.833-7.5 s (mean 2.40 s), 1.999 h in total. No speaker, gender or transcript information. The Kaggle release contains three versions; versions 1 and 1.1 are the same 1,200 clips with 4 emotions, different from the 3,000 clips of 1.2. Comparing 350 wav files of version 1.1 with 1.2: of a random 200, 115 (57.5%) are byte-identical to 1.2 files, and 81 of those 115 have a different label (e.g. none of the 19 that were sad in 1.1 is sad in 1.2). In version 1.2, 12 pairs (24 clips) of nearly the same sound of the same line in the same film have different labels. Three Fleiss' kappas exist: 0.6713 (README of 1.2), 0.6338 (README of 1/1.1), 0.61 (paper abstract), for different sets. The paper's abstract (IEEE Access 2026) describes the 4-emotion version; no paper for the 6-emotion version 1.2 was found.

name: Harper Valley Bank
full_title: Harper Valley Bank Spoken Dialog Corpus
status_note: Simulated call-centre recordings. Implemented with per-segment polarity (negative/neutral/positive). Labels are the output of Gridspace's emotion model (automatic), not human. Segments without speech (human transcript empty or tags only) also carry labels and are excluded. Intents and dialogue acts are not used.
license_note: The repository's `LICENSE` is the full text of Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International. "How to Cite" in the README gives the BibTeX of arXiv:2010.13929.
release_version: GitHub cricketclub/gridspace-stanford-harper-valley commit 0bd721e877c4a85d8c13ff837e68661ea6200a98 (2021-03-12). The recipe downloads the master tarball (676,302,876 bytes)
labels_discrete_note: Polarity, not emotion. Each segment's `emotion` is a softmax over negative/neutral/positive (summing to 1.0), and the arg-max is the label (ties to 0). Arg-max over all 25,730 segments: neutral 17,149 / positive 8,148 / negative 433. In the 19,456 segments used by the recipe (6,274 without speech removed): neutral 10,960 / positive 8,080 / negative 416. The median confidence (max probability) of negative arg-maxes is 0.492, a weak decision. positive is frequent in agents' greetings and closings, and some negative examples are lexically neutral (`i need to check my account balance`).
label_basis_note: Crowd workers were assigned the role of a bank customer or agent and talked by phone following a goal and a rough script (role-play, no emotion instruction). Sentiment polarity (negative / neutral / positive) is an automatic estimate by the Gridspace Speech API, not a human annotation.
lexical_confound_note: Task-oriented role-play (rough script, no per-sentence design); sentiment labels come from a model whose inputs (audio or text) are not documented, so the words may drive the labels. Human transcripts exist, so a check is possible but was not made.
annotations_other: Intents, dialogue acts (16 kinds), transcripts. Sentiment polarity is an automatic label (probabilities) from Gridspace's speech API.
notes: Wu, Nafziger, Scodary, Maas (Gridspace and Stanford). 1,446 simulated call-centre calls, 59 speakers (in agent and caller roles). One call = 2 wav files (one per side, 8 kHz mono PCM_16). Human transcripts by trained Gridspace Mixer workers. Segmentation follows the word times of Gridspace's automatic speech recognition (paper: "automatic segmentation"). In all 25,730 segments `duration_ms` matches the end of the last word of the machine transcript. Measured disagreements with the README: `duration_ms` is described as the call length but is the segment length; `offset_ms` does not match the audio position (`start_ms` does); `channel_index` (1 = caller, 2 = agent) and `speaker_role` are swapped in 37 calls (596 segments), and the voice is in the wav on the `channel_index` side (confirmed by listening and audio energy). Differences from Table 1 of the paper: words per utterance, paper mean 4.1 and median 4.5, measured (`human_transcript`) mean 5.64 and median 4.0; utterances per call, paper 2-60, measured 3-76 (the mean 17.79 matches). `hours_reported` 23.7 corresponds to the one-side total (measured 23.655 h); both sides total 47.311 h and segments total 12.024 h. 349 segments have an empty human transcript and 5,925 only tags such as `[noise]`. The corpus has no speaker gender, age or other attributes. Simulated calls (crowd workers phoning from scripts), with vocabulary limited to about 700 words: scripted, acted conversation rather than real customers' emotions. Labels are the output of Gridspace's automatic model, not human, and no human verification is described (neither the paper nor the README gives the model's name, version, training data or accuracy). Whether to use it for training or only for evaluation is the recipe side's (maintainer's) decision, still open.

name: LEGOv2
status_note: Implemented with 5 classes (angry / friendly / neutral / slightly_angry / very_angry); uses 4,243 of the 4,832 labelled utterances (291 of 302 calls, 1.97 h). The 589 'garbage' utterances are left out because the maintainer's listening found silence or content that cannot be labelled (2026-10-25; a few were heard, not all). The 4 'friendly' utterances are kept as a class. Labels are one rater's judgement of anger; this is an anger-detection corpus, not a general multi-emotion one. 8 kHz telephone speech.
license_note: license.txt in the release lists two licenses, both: 'Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to use this data and its documentation for individual, education research purposes only.' (Carnegie Mellon University, 2003-2015, for the recorded data and transcriptions; Ulm University, 2009-2015, for the annotations). Redistribution is not mentioned. The readme asks to cite Schmitt, Ultes and Minker (LREC 2012) and Ultes et al. (IWSDS 2015).
labels_discrete_note: friendly, neutral, slightly angry, angry, very angry (one rater, 302 calls). The release also contains 'garbage' (589 utterances), which is not in the scheme and is not used. Counts of the 4,832 labelled utterances: neutral 3,305; slightly angry 693; garbage 589; angry 137; very angry 104; friendly 4.
label_basis_note: One rater judged the callers' emotional state (friendly, neutral, slightly angry, angry, very angry) for 302 calls; the readme does not say whether the rater listened to the audio or read the dialogue. The release also holds a value 'garbage' (589 utterances) that the readme does not define; the maintainer listened to several and found silence or content that cannot be labelled, so the recipe leaves them out.
lexical_confound_note: Anger labels come from one rater who may have read the dialogue as well as heard the callers (not stated). ASR text of each utterance is in interactions.csv, so a text-only check is possible but was not made.
annotations_other: dialogue-act and interaction annotations
sheet_notes: Derived from CMU Let's Go spoken-dialogue data and annotated for anger detection. This is not a general multi-emotion SER corpus. Exact corpus size and license terms require checking the downloadable license file.
notes: Parameterized and annotated spoken dialogue corpus of the CMU Let's Go bus information system (Schmitt, Ultes and Minker, LREC 2012; Ultes et al., IWSDS 2015); interactions from 2006 and 2007, annotated at Ulm University. Archive 1.19 GB from the University of Bamberg server, no official checksum. 7,909 wav: user utterances (mostly 8 kHz mono 16-bit, one 44.1 kHz) and whole-call recordings up to 1,332 s. interactions.csv holds 13,835 exchanges with 53 interaction parameters, ASR results, dialogue acts and the emotional state; 4,832 have an emotion label and an audio file. The release also has Interaction Quality annotations (401 calls, 9,638 exchanges, several raters), calls.csv (gender, age, outcome per call), acoustics.csv (Praat features) and a MySQL dump, none of which the recipe uses. Utterances are short (median 1.1 s). Two groups of byte-identical files (533 files, copies of one call folder) are not among the used utterances. The language is English.

name: Lithuanian Emotional Speech Database (Emocijų duomenų bazė)
status_note: Implemented with 8 classes (the 7 README emotions plus longing); uses all 1,453 clips. The license is not stated and the authors are to be asked (not yet contacted). The README describes 10 actors x 100 phrases x 7 emotions (7,000 recordings), but the repository holds 1,453, unevenly spread (4 to 98 clips per speaker and emotion); whether the rest exists is unknown.
license_note: The repository (BPTI-LT/Emociju-duomenu-baze, commit 526844b9, last pushed 2018-05-03) has no LICENSE file and GitHub shows no license; the README holds a description only, with no license or citation request. Terms for research use, redistribution and commercial use are unknown. The maintainer will ask the authors (2026-10-25; not yet contacted) and, until then, does not redistribute or use it commercially.
labels_discrete_note: Folder names are Lithuanian: Baime (fear), Pyktis (anger), Dziaugsmas (happiness), Nuostaba (surprise), Pasislykstejimas (disgust), Liudesys (sadness), Neutrali (neutral). Speaker 5 also has a folder Ilgesys (9 clips), a word that means longing and is not among the README's seven emotions; the recipe uses it as an eighth class, longing (maintainer's decision, 2026-10-25).
label_basis_note: Label = the emotion the non-professional actor was reading in (folder name). The README describes no verification.
lexical_confound_note: By design every phrase is read in every emotion; in the release the same phrase number appears under several emotions within a speaker. Only about a fifth of the designed recordings (1,453 of 7,000) are present and the phrase texts are missing, so this was not checked on the wording itself.
notes: Recorded in the study 'Let's teach the Computer to Feel (Recognize Emotions in the Human Voice)' of the Mokslo pieva project (BPTI-LT, 2018). 10 non-professional actors read 100 phrases in seven emotions (README). Archive of 1,453 wav (44.1 kHz mono 16-bit, 2.357-8.167 s, 1.6598 h) in folders EMOdb/<n> Zmogus/<n> <Emotion>/<Emotion>_<phrase number>.wav. Counts per speaker and emotion range from 4 to 98 (e.g. speaker 1: 98 Pyktis and 10 Baime; speaker 10: 94 Dziaugsmas). Class counts: sadness 342, happiness 260, neutral 245, anger 239, disgust 150, surprise 105, fear 103, longing 9. No gender, age or phrase texts are given. No byte-identical files.

name: MaSERC
full_title: MaSERC: A Dual-Scenario Marathi Emotional Speech Corpus for Speech Emotion Recognition Research
status_note: Implemented with 6 classes (angry / fear / happy / neutral / sad / surprise); uses 772 of the 808 clips. Left out: 5 zero-length wav, 27 byte-identical copies and 4 clips whose labels disagree between copies; 7 pairs of identical recordings (14 clips) are kept (maintainer's decision), and 6 of those pairs fall in different splits. The maintainer's light listening found the emotional expression weak. The files are 44.1 kHz stereo (the description says 16 kHz mono) and total 0.82 h (the description says 68 min).
language_note: Marathi (dialect backgrounds such as Pune, Vidarbha, Marathwada, Konkan)
license_note: Mendeley Data license field: CC BY 4.0 (re-read through the Mendeley API, 2026-10-26; checked by the maintainer).
label_basis_note: Label = the emotion in the file name (the emotion the speaker was to deliver). The description reports a majority-vote validation by three annotators (kappa >= 0.78); their individual votes are not distributed.
lexical_confound_note: Scenario 1 uses one sentence in all emotions (no lexical information). Scenario 2 is a monologue whose six sentences each embed a different emotion in a fixed order, so for those clips the words indicate the emotion. The release does not say which clips belong to which scenario and has no transcripts.
paralinguistic_signal_note: The maintainer listened lightly (a few clips) on 2026-10-25 and could not hear a typical paralinguistic expression of the labelled emotions; the cause (acting skill, cultural difference) is not known. The description's validation by three annotators (kappa >= 0.78) may argue against a real problem.
notes: MaSERC (Marathi Speech Emotion Recognition Corpus), MIT Art, Design and Technology University, Pune; Mendeley Data b9jrrpdxgb version 1, 2026-06-22, one 285 MB zip. Native Marathi speakers (students and a few staff, aged 18-50, several dialect backgrounds), recorded in a partially controlled indoor room with a condenser microphone. Two scenarios (carrier sentence once per emotion; six-sentence exam monologue with one emotion per sentence). The description promises predefined splits, speaker metadata and scenario labels, but the release holds only 808 wav files. File names look like '<series> <number>[ name]-<Emotion>-<take>.wav' (the description gives another form); the emotion word is spelled in several ways (case, surpsise, Surprsie, suprise) and 11 names do not parse. 44.1 kHz stereo (42 files float), median 3.9 s, up to 12.3 s, 0.8214 h. 5 zero-length wav, 30 groups of byte-identical files (63 files), and 17 pairs of equal names holding different recordings. Speaker names appear in some file names and are not recorded here.

lexical_confound_note: Nonverbal affect bursts with no linguistic content, one per actor and emotion (10 per emotion).
notes: Belin, Fillion-Bilodeau and Gosselin (Behavior Research Methods 40(2), 2008), deposited on Zenodo 2025-09-02 (3 files: Sounds.zip 7.6 MB, Sounds.csv, the paper PDF). 90 nonverbal affect bursts by 10 actors (5 male, 5 female) for 8 emotions plus neutral: anger, disgust, fear, pain, sadness, surprise, happiness, pleasure, neutral; 10 clips per label. 44.1 kHz mono 16-bit, 0.240-4.310 s, 0.0272 h. Sounds.csv holds F0 (min, max, median, SD), duration and power (median, SD) per clip; its Duration_ms column mixes units (41 rows in seconds, 49 in milliseconds). Ratings of valence, arousal and intensity by 30 participants are not distributed per clip.

name: MELD
status_note: Implemented with 7 classes (angry / disgust / fear / happy / neutral / sad / surprise); uses 13,704 of the 13,708 utterances (4 left out: a corrupt mp4, a missing mp4, and two whose CSV time interval is 305 s and 235 s). 43 groups (91 clips) of identical or near-identical sound are kept for now and are to be removed later (24 groups carry different emotions, 3 span the official train and test splits). Labels are the majority of three annotators who also saw the video, not judgements of the voice alone.
license_note: GitHub license of declare-lab/MELD: GPL-3.0 (re-read 2026-10-26; the DB records GPL-3.0-only). The material is clips of the TV series Friends, and the README states no rights for it. A footnote of the paper (ACL 2019) says the authors consulted a legal office to verify that use and distribution of very short videos fall under fair use (read and confirmed by the maintainer, 2026-10-26).
label_basis_note: Label = the majority of three annotators (graduate students) who judged each utterance with the video clip available (Section 3.1; Fleiss kappa 0.43). The original EmotionLines annotation had only the transcripts. The labels therefore are not judgements of the voice alone.
lexical_confound_note: Emotion labels come from annotators who understood the words and saw the video (and the original EmotionLines labels came from transcripts alone), so the wording of an utterance probably carries information about its label. Not measured.
annotations_other: sentiment labels (positive, negative, neutral)
sheet_notes: Multimodal conversational emotion dataset derived from Friends. The repository and Hugging Face distribution declare GPL-3.0, but the license scope and redistribution rights for the underlying television clips are not explicitly documented. GitHub Issue #9 reports audio disturbances affecting roughly 200 training videos (especially files larger than 2.5 MB) and multiple video-text mismatch or synchronization errors. File-level quality control, documented exclusions, and split-preserving checks are required before acoustic or multimodal evaluation: https://github.com/declare-lab/MELD/issues/9. Reported duration varies with preprocessing; 12.1 hours is used here. Although MELD includes many speakers, its utterance distribution is highly skewed because most of the data comes from the six main characters.
notes: Audio is extracted from MP4 (mostly 6-channel AAC, converted to mono). Speakers are Friends character names (304, skewed to the six main characters). Has sentiment (positive/negative/neutral), Dialogue_ID, Season, Episode and timestamps. GitHub Issue #9 reports corrupted audio in about 200 training videos. The CSV files hold 13,708 utterances (train 9,989, valid 1,109, test 2,610); emotions: neutral 6,436, joy 2,308, surprise 1,636, anger 1,607, sadness 1,002, disgust 361, fear 358. The release has 2,060 macOS '._' stub files, one unreadable mp4, one CSV row without an mp4 and 141 mp4 without a CSV row. The four utterances left out are train Ross dia125 utt3 (corrupt mp4), valid Phoebe dia110 utt7 (no mp4), and test Student dia38 utt4 (305 s) and Phoebe dia220 utt0 (235 s), whose CSV intervals cover minutes of audio under one label. Groups of identical sound (from the review, not recomputed here): 43 groups and 91 clips, 24 of them with different emotions in the group (for example four utterances of one test dialogue labelled neutral, happy, angry and angry), probably neighbouring cuts with overlapping subtitle times (a guess), and 3 spanning the official train and test splits (train dia12 utt7 and 8 with test dia85 utt0 and 1; train dia887 utt0 with test dia117 utt8).

name: MER2024
full_title: MER 2024: Semi-Supervised Learning, Noise Robustness, and Open-Vocabulary Multimodal Emotion Recognition
status_note: Data of the challenge that extends MER2023. Gated on Hugging Face (value: auto), asking for a form and a non-commercial agreement. Added at the request of the literature database (2026-10-23).

notes: Lian et al. (MRAC workshop at ACM MM 2024). The 5,030 Train&Val clips are all the labelled clips of MER2023 (§2). MER-SEMI and MER-NOISE each have about 1,170 clips chosen from 115,595 unlabelled clips where at least 4 of 5 annotators agreed. MER-NOISE adds noise to the audio and blurs the video. The Hugging Face release has video, subtitles (Chinese and English), discrete labels, EMER descriptions (332 clips) and open-vocabulary labels.

name: MER2025
status_note: The type of procedure comes from the spreadsheet Notes (approval and EULA); not checked individually. Made a candidate on 2026-10-14 under the revised policy (maintainer's decision: manual access steps, label types and automatic labels are not reasons to exclude).

MER-SEMI contains 132,171 samples (7,369 labeled and 124,802 unlabeled); MER-FG uses OV-MERD and MER-Caption+; MER-PR uses MDPE with 233 participants. No single comparable total-hours or speaker count is available. Access requires approval under a customized CC BY-NC 4.0 license plus EULA, with no redistribution or modification.
notes: Paper arXiv 2504.19423 (ACM MM 2025): the EULA allows academic research only, forbids modification and re-uploading, and strictly forbids human annotation of MER2025 samples. The Hugging Face release also contains training CSVs for MER-Caption, MER-Caption+ and OV-MERD (track2/track3). Hugging Face gated value: auto (2026-10-23).

name: MSP-Podcast
status_note: A recipe exists in egs3 (recipes.csv)
annotations_other: speaker and source metadata
sheet_notes: Version 2.0 contains 409 hours and 264,705 speaking turns. The published partition-level speaker counts sum to 3,929 (Train 2,220 + Development 704 + Test1 465 + Test2 112 + Test3 428). This is not a verified unique-speaker total: the official page notes speaker overlap among the test sets, and train samples without speaker identity may belong to test speakers. Treat 3,929 as the sum of reported partition counts, not as a lower bound on unique speakers. Access requires an academic license agreement; podcast-level source licenses and the hidden Test3 labels must be considered separately.
notes: The recipe uses release 2.0 and evaluates on Test1/Test2. It does not download; it points to Audios/ and Labels/Labels/labels_consensus.csv obtained by the user. Paper arXiv 2509.09791v1: 1,446,270 annotations by 13,280 annotators. The primary-emotion agreement of 0.411 is called Cohen's kappa in the title of Table III and Fleiss' kappa in §VI (inconsistent within the paper). naturalvoices extends the same source podcast recordings to all speaker turns (5,049 hours; arXiv 2511.00256).

name: NonverbalTTS
full_title: NonverbalTTS: A Public English Corpus of Text-Aligned Nonverbal Vocalizations with Emotion Annotations for Text-to-Speech
status_note: Audio is cut from VoxCeleb and Expresso. Emotions were classified automatically by emotion2vec+ large and reviewed by annotators, who replaced them where needed. Implemented (for evaluation only). The public split other, the emotion other and untagged clips are not used.
license_note: Hugging Face card text: annotations under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; audio under the licenses of the sources (VoxCeleb, Expresso). The Hugging Face metadata field says apache-2.0, which disagrees with the text and is not adopted (maintainer's decision). Expresso is CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://speechbot.github.io/expresso/). VoxCeleb's vox1 page at VGG gives CC BY-SA 4.0 for the "metadata" (nothing about the audio itself). Evaluation use only.
labels_discrete_note: One emotion per clip: emotion2vec+ large's automatic classification reviewed by 3 annotators (paper §3.2, §3.3). Details of human involvement and label reliability unverified. Overall: neutral 2,406 / happy 1,605 / other 1,177 / sad 387 / disgusted 78 / surprised 34 / angry 25 / fearful 10 / untagged 534 (matches paper Table 6; untagged means annotators disagreed, about 8.5% per paper §4.2). other is an ambiguous category outside the 8 emotions (paper §4.2).
label_basis_note: Audio cut from VoxCeleb (natural speech such as interviews) and Expresso (actors' read and improvised performances). Emotions were classified automatically into 8 classes by emotion2vec+ large; annotators listened and replaced them where needed (Argilla; annotators were given definitions of each emotion). The number of raters and how judgements were combined are not described. Expresso's style tags are not used.
lexical_confound_note: VoxCeleb part is unscripted interview speech. For the Expresso part, the relation between text and labels, and whether annotators saw transcripts, are not described and were not measured.
annotations_other: Transcripts with positions of 10 non-verbal vocalisations (breathing, laughter, sigh, sneeze, cough, throat clearing, groan, grunt, snore, sniff), DNSMOS, speaker ID. NVs are embedded in the transcript as emoji (the mapping from symbols to types is inferred from the counts in paper Table 2; the official table was not obtained)
notes: Borisov et al. (SSW 2025), deepvk. 17 hours, 2,296 speakers. Hugging Face splits: train 3,641, dev 46, test 359, other 2,210 (6,256 rows in total). The paper's splits are only train/dev/test (Table 5; the paper's train is 3,642, one more than measured). The public split other (2,210 clips) is not explained by the paper or card and is not used in the official experiments. It carries emotion and other annotations, but the recipe does not use it. Measured: 1,373 of the 1,378 clips without NVs and 522 of the 534 untagged clips are in other, and the share with transcripts from all 3 annotators is low (47%, vs 75-84% in the other splits). The public split other and the emotion label other are different things. Audio: 4,452 clips from VoxCeleb (13.68 h, 16 kHz) and 1,804 from Expresso (3.91 h, 48 kHz), distinguishable by the data_name column. The train and test counts of paper Table 7 (emotions per split) do not match the measurements. Of the 6,256 clips (17.59 h), the recipe uses 3,201 (8.12 h), excluding the public split other (2,210), emotion other (833) and untagged (12); NVs are not used because a clip can contain several (multi-label). Position (maintainer's decision): evaluation only. The VoxCeleb part is in-the-wild YouTube audio, an evaluation set close to YODAS, worth looking at separately. The Expresso part is read and improvised dialogue of a different nature. Emotion labels are automatic classification plus annotator review; their reliability needs checking.

name: ReCANVo
full_title: ReCANVo: A Database of Real-World Communicative and Affective Nonverbal Vocalizations
status_note: 7,077 non-verbal vocalisations of 8 minimally speaking people, labelled with their meaning on the spot by family members. Many labels are emotion words (delighted, frustrated, dysregulated, ...), mixed with communicative intents. Implemented. `laugh` is merged into `laughter`, giving 21 classes.
license_note: Zenodo license field: CC BY 3.0 US. The Zenodo description asks for the paper Johnson & Narain et al. (Sci Data 10, 523, 2023, doi 10.1038/s41597-023-02405-7) to be cited.
labels_discrete_note: 6 labels shared by all participants (delighted, dysregulated, frustrated, request, self-talk, social) and up to 4 individual labels chosen by the family from 25 options (paper, Methods). Labels were assigned on the spot by family members (one label per vocalisation). The CSV has 22 kinds (self-talk written `selftalk`): selftalk 1885, frustrated 1536, delighted 1272, dysregulated 704, social 634, request 419, affectionate 129, yes 123, laughter 93, dysregulation-sick 74, happy 61, help 24, more 22, protest 21, bathroom 20, dysregulation-bathroom 18, no 12, glee 8, laugh 8, tablet 7, hunger 4, greeting 3. Paper Table 2 has 21 kinds, without `laugh` (8 clips, all P03). Participant x label counts match Table 2 except one cell: P03 laughter (8) in Table 2, while the CSV has 0 `laughter` and 8 `laugh` for P03. Following the paper, they are treated as the same label (maintainer's decision).
label_basis_note: Non-verbal vocalisations produced in daily life (home, school, etc.) by people with very little spoken language. Labels were assigned on the spot by a parent or caregiver who knew the person well (real time, one person, judging with full view of the situation). Labels include intents such as requests as well as emotions.
lexical_confound_note: Non-verbal vocalisations of people with about 0-10 spoken words, so there are almost no words to learn from (a few clips may contain words; not checked).
notes: Johnson & Narain et al. (MIT Media Lab, Scientific Data 2023). 8 participants (paper Tables 1 and 2: 6 male, 2 female), aged 6-23, with diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder, cerebral palsy or genetic conditions. Wearable recordings at home and school. The paper calls people with about 0-10 spoken words minimally speaking (the Zenodo description says non-speaking). Measured: 7,077 clips, 2.461 h, 0.082-14.057 s (median 0.949 s). The Zenodo description says "approximately 0.5-4 seconds", but 1,043 clips are under 0.5 s and 169 over 4 s. Audio is 44.1 kHz (the paper says 16-bit), mixed: 4,281 mono, 2,796 stereo; 5,466 PCM_16, 1,611 PCM_32. Clips per participant: P01 1,708 / P08 1,545 / P05 1,028 / P16 779 / P06 569 / P02 557 / P03 525 / P11 366. The bundled `Communication_Profiles.xlsx` (participant questionnaire, not clip labels) covers only 7 people and lacks P02 (the paper says a separate .csv, but the release has .xlsx). File names follow the paper's format, with 38 exceptions. Of the 7,077 clips, the recipe uses 7,051, excluding 26 train/valid clips under 0.2 s (WavLM's SpecAugment fails under 0.205 s; the maintainer listened to the 29 clips under 0.2 s and agreed to exclude them). Position: everyday non-verbal sounds of people with little speech; labels are a mix of emotions and communicative intents assigned by family members. Whether speaker-specific voices confuse training is unverified. Inclusion in multi-corpus training is undecided (idea: include it, and if time allows compare with a version without it).

labels_discrete_note: Labels are only the emotion codes in file names (an / di / fe / ha / sa / su), 120 each, 720 in total. The per-file emotion is the instruction to the performer; the Kaggle description says only samples for which all of at least two listeners who did not know the language perceived the intended emotion were taken for experiments (about 500 samples). Neither the test results nor a mark of which ~500 files are in the release. The recipe uses 714 clips after removing 6 with identical md5.

notes: Ryerson Multimedia Lab (Wang & Guan, IEEE Trans. Multimedia 2008, etc.). 8 subjects, 6 languages (Kaggle description: English, Mandarin, Urdu, Punjabi, Persian, Italian). The description's audio specification is 22,050 Hz, single channel, 16-bit, video 30 fps, but the actual files are PCM 16-bit stereo inside avi, 669 at 44.1 kHz and 51 at 48 kHz (the two channels differ in all 720). 2.13-8.37 s (mean 4.94 s), 0.987 h in total. The release has 720 avi files, which does not match the description's "about 500 samples". 5 groups (11 clips) have identical md5 (within the same subject, folder and emotion; the maintainer listened and confirmed the audio is the same utterance; the recipe keeps only the lowest-numbered one and excludes the other 6). The release has no label files other than the emotion codes in file names, no transcripts and no listening-test results. An acted audio-visual database. Only 8 subjects, and the split is by subject folder, so the emotion make-up of each split is skewed (e.g. valid has 8 angry and 18 happy). Since the license is Unknown, how to use it (evaluation only, etc.) awaits the team's confirmation.

sheet_notes: SUBESCO is an audio-only emotional speech corpus of 7000 sentence-level utterances of the Bangla language. 20 professional actors (10 males and 10 females) participated in the recordings of 10 sentences for 7 target emotions. The emotions are Anger, Disgust, Fear, Happiness, Neutral, Sadness and Surprise. Total duration of the corpus is 7 hours 40 min 40 sec.  Total size of the dataset is 2.03 GB. The dataset was evaluated by 50 raters (25 males, 25 females). Human perception test achieved a raw accuracy of 71%.  All the details relating to creation, evaluation and analysis of SUBESCO have been described in the corresponding journal paper which has been published in Plos One.
notes: All information is in the file names (gender, speaker number, speaker name, sentence number, emotion, take). Reproducibility over 5 takes can be measured. Transcripts are not bundled; the paper lists the 10 sentences. The listening experiment (50 people, 71% accuracy) is reported only as aggregates in the paper. No official split; speakers are assigned in equal numbers per gender.
